## Introduction

### Overview

This session introduces basics of [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) - its
three components **YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) header**, **code
chunks** and **text**. We will learn to create Quarto document, use
several options to display/hide codes and figures and render Quarto
document to html document.

### Learning goals

In this session, you will learn:

-   Basics of **Quarto (syntax and formats)**
-   How to create and render a Quarto document in RStudio
-   Understand three components of Quarto ; YAML header, code chunks and
    text

## Quarto

Quarto is the next-generation version of R Markdown that allows to
combine prose, code, results. Quarto is not limited to single
programming language but is available in R, Python, Julia and
Observable. Here, we will focus to use Quarto in RStudio.

Quarto documents are reproducible and support different output formats
such as PDFs, Microsoft Word files, presentations and many more.

**Advantages of using Quarto:**

1.  Communicate with your collaborator: It includes code, results and
    steps/narrative in a single document
2.  Supports multi-format outputs such as HTML, PDF, Markdown, websites
    and more
3.  Reproducibility of research

**Note: Quarto is a command-line interface tool but not R package.
Therefore, you do not need to install it separately. Rstudio has
integrated Quarto to work with R.** **However, there is an R package
`quarto` that allows to call Quarto from R console.**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Install Quarto R package
install.packages("quarto")
```

### Open new Quarto document in Rstudio

Quarto file is a plain text file with `.qmd` extension. To create a new
Quarto document: `File` \> `New File` \> `Quarto Document`
![](../img/quarto_file_open.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"}

This will open a new window with several options. We can select the
Quarto outputs such as Documents, Presentation, interactive in different
formats. For example, for documents, we can pick HTML, PDF or Word
format. We can even choose Engine Knitr or Jupyter.

![](../img/new_quarto_doc.png){width="60%" fig-align="center"} This will
create an new unamed `Untitled.qmd` file. Lets rename it, by going to
`File`, `Save As` and `name of the file`.

## Components of Quarto:

1.  The YAML header surrounded by (`---`)
2.  Code chunk surrounded by (\`\`\`{r})
3.  Text- explanation of results

### YAML header

The header for the Quarto document is written in **YAML language**. It
allows to specify themes, formats, executable options and many more.
Additionally, it consists of series of metadata such as title, author
date etc. You can think of YAML header as the settings of the Quarto
document on how to process and present your document. It is surrounded
by (`---`), at the top of the Quarto document. A simple example of YAML
header is shown below: ![](../img/yaml_header.png){width="80%"
fig-align="center"}

We can add some additional contents to the YAML header such as authors,
date, table of content and set the theme
![](../img/yaml_header_1.png){width="40%" fig-align="center"}

Some of the additional contents of the YAML header can be found
[here](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html)

### Code chunks

**Code chunks** is a section to write and execute the code. It is
enclosed in a three back ticks followed by `r`. You can write multiple
line of codes inside the code chunks.
![](../img/code_chunk.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

**Code chunks can be added in three different ways in RStudio**

1.  Keyboard commands: `Ctrl-Alt-I` (Windows) or `Cmd-Option-I` (Mac)

2.  Typing it manually \`\`\``{r}` followed by three back ticks \`\`\`
    at the end of the chunk

3.  Clicking the insert button in the toolbar and select R

    ![](../img/insert_code_chunk.png){width="50%" fig-align="center"}

-   We can include comment inside the code chunk using the `#` symbol
    (**similar to bash**).
-   Triangle sign with a line below execute all the code chunks before
    the current chunk.
-   Triangle sign facing towards right (similar to play button) runs the
    current chunk.

#### Chunk options

Several options can be added to your code chunk to customize the output
of code. Some of the commonly used chunk options are:

-   `echo: FALSE` runs your code chunk, displays output, but does not
    display code in your final doc (this is useful if you want to show a
    figure but not the code used to create it)

-   `eval: FALSE` does not run your code, but does display it in your
    final doc

-   `include: FALSE` runs your code but does not display the code or its
    output in your final doc

-   `message: FALSE` prevents messages from showing up in your final doc

-   `warning: FALSE` prevents earnings from showing up in your final doc

-   `fig.height: X` and `fig.width: Y` will allow you to specify the
    dimensions of your figures (in inches)

-   `fig.align:` can be set to “left”, “right”, or “center”

-   `fig.cap:` "Your figure caption" will allow you to set a figure
    caption

-   `fig.alt:` "Your alt text" will allow you to set alt text for screen
    readers

-   `cache: TRUE` will cache results, meaning if you have a chunk that
    takes a long time to run, if you haven’t changed anything and you
    knit again, the code won’t run again but access the cache.

-   `fig-show=hide` to hide the figures

More chunk options can be found \[here\]
(https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html/). Chunk
options can be either written directly inside the `curly braces`
(similar to the R Markdown) or by using `#| (YAML syntax)` before the
code chunk where each `#|` line sets one option.

```{r echo=TRUE}
# Example code chunk
2*2
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
2*3
```

#### Chunk labels

Chunks can be labelled in Quarto using `#| label: chunk-name` before the
code chunk. The chunk name should be unique and cannot contain spaces.

**Advantages of labeling chunks:**

-   It helps to refer the chunk in other places such as
    cross-referencing.
-   You can set up a network of certain chunks not to rerun to avoid the
    computational time.

```{r}
#| label: my-first-chunk
2 + 3
```

```{r}
#| label: my-second-chunk
5 * 6
```

#### Run the code chunk:

1.  Click the green play button
2.  Keyboard shortcut: `Ctrl-Shift-Enter` (Windows) or `Cmd-Shift-Enter`
    (Mac)
3.  Place the cursor inside the chunk and press `Ctrl-Enter` (Windows)
    or `Cmd-Enter` (Mac)

### Markdown text

The default text for the Quarto is Markdown, unlike R, where everything
is considered code until commented out by `#`. Therefore, you can
directly write the text outside the code chunks. Quarto text syntax is
based on Pandoc Markdown which is similar to original Markdown syntax we
discussed in
[Week02](https://mcic-osu.github.io/pracs-au25/week02/w2b_vscode-markdown.html)

#### Headings

Headings are created by using `#` followed by a space and the heading.
Quarto supports six levels of headings.

Visual editor:

Source editor: Example 1:

**Inline code- The R code can be directly added in the text using single
back ticks followed by `r` such as `r 2+2` which will produce `r 2+2` in
the output document.**

### Render a Quarto document

Rendering a Quarto document converts the `.qmd` document to the
requested format **(html/pdf or any other format)**. During rendering,
Quarto document(`.qmd`) is first processed using the **knitr** and then
converted to the final format using **pandoc**. While rendering, all the
code chunks are executed and the output is embedded in the final
document with the text. **However, if there are any codes that produces
error, your document will not be rendered.** To render a Quarto
document, click on the `Render` button.
![](../img/render.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

**Other options to render Quarto document:**

-   Press `Ctrl-Shift-K` (Windows) or `Cmd-Shift-K` (Mac) to render the
    document.
-   Use command `quarto::quarto_render("filename.qmd")` in the console.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
quarto::quarto_render("first_quarto_document.qmd")
```

There is an option to render automatically when you save. I would not
personally prefer to click it because if you are doing some
computationally intensive task, it will keep rendering.

**Visualize output:** You can visualize output either in the separate
window or viewer pan. The gear icon next to the Render would help to
change the setting of output visualization.

## Global option

You can change the default option of the chunk. Suppose you want to show
just the figures and table without showing the command that produces it.
You can do it in the Quarto YAML header under execute, by adding the
following global option:`execute: echo :false`.

## Practice

1. Create a PDF by saving the Quarto(.qmd) file you created to save your
script.
2. Add the following to the YAML header of your Quarto document:
   - Author name
   - Date
   - Table of contents
   - Theme
3. Load the package `palmerpenguins` installed in `week11` exercise and save the 
`penguins` data in a object called penguin_data.
4. Create a scatter plot of `flipper_length_mm` (x-axis) and
`body_mass_g` (y-axis) colored by `species` using `ggplot2` package.
5. Customize the figure by adding figure caption, changing the figure
dimensions (height and width) and aligning it to the center.
6. Add a text section explaining the figure you created above.
